## Understanding the problem

We must implement `carArrived` so that cars on the same road may cross freely, but cars from the two different roads never cross simultaneously, and we never call `turnGreen` when the light is already green on that road. The light starts green on road A (roadId 1) and red on road B.

**Example 1:** Cars 1, 3, 5 all arrive on road A while it is green — they cross immediately with no `turnGreen` calls. Then car 2 arrives on road B: since the light is green for A, we flip it (`turnGreen`) and print "Traffic Light On Road B Is Green", then car 2 and later car 4 cross without further flips.

**Example 2:** Car 1 crosses on A. Car 2 flips to B and crosses; car 3 follows on B. Car 5 arrives on road A but car 4 (road B) is also active — one of them flips the light, waits for the other to finish, then crosses. Both orderings are accepted; the key is mutual exclusion plus flipping only on a real change.

Constraints are tiny (≤ 20 cars), so any correct synchronization scheme works; the challenge is purely about concurrency correctness, not performance.
k: A single lock guarding both 'which road is green' state and the crossing itself guarantees mutual exclusion and prevents deadlocks.
Only call turnGreen when the currently green road differs from the arriving car's road.
An atomic integer holding the green road id allows a lock-free solution via compare-and-swap.

a.i: Keep a shared variable `greenRoad` (initially 1). Every call to `carArrived` acquires a global mutex, checks whether `greenRoad` equals the incoming `roadId`; if not, calls `turnGreen()` and updates the variable. Then release the lock before calling `crossCar()`. Because all state inspection and light-flipping happen under one lock, no two cars from different roads can be in their critical section at once, and `turnGreen` is never called redundantly.
s: Initialize shared state: greenRoad = 1 and a mutex.
If greenRoad != roadId, call turnGreen() and set greenRoad = roadId.
Unlock the mutex, then call crossCar().
a.t: O(1) per car — constant work under the lock, O(n) total for n cars.
a.sp: O(1) — one integer and one lock.

a.n: Approach 2: Lock-free with an atomic variable
a.i: Store the id of the green road in an atomic integer initialized to 1. Each car uses compare-and-swap semantics: atomically read the current value; if it already matches its road, just cross. Otherwise attempt to swap in its own road id — the thread whose CAS succeeds performs `turnGreen`, and everyone else sees the updated value afterward. This removes the explicit mutex while preserving the invariant that exactly one road is green and `turnGreen` fires only on transitions.
s: Read the current value of greenRoad.
If it equals roadId, skip straight to crossCar().
Otherwise atomically exchange greenRoad with roadId; if the old value differed, call turnGreen().
a.t: O(1) per car — a single atomic exchange plus callbacks.

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it is the canonical answer, easy to explain, and clearly deadlock-free because there is a single lock and no nested acquisition. Mention Approach 2 as a refinement showing fluency with atomics. Common pitfalls: calling `turnGreen` unconditionally (fails the "already green" check), forgetting to update the stored green-road id after flipping, or holding the lock across `crossCar` unnecessarily (still correct here, but coarser than needed). Edge cases: the very first car always finds road A green; consecutive cars on the same road must not trigger extra `turnGreen` calls. Likely follow-ups: extend to N roads with round-robin fairness, add priority/starvation-freedom guarantees, or model the problem with semaphores or condition variables instead of a plain mutex.
